claim_verdicts.evidence: using_helm: "Note that installing a chart creates a new release object." changes_since_helm2: in Helm 2 "once a name was used by a release, no other release could use that same name"; Helm 3 scopes release names to the namespace. helm_uninstall: "It removes all of the resources associated with the last release of the chart" (objects tracked together). Pages are Helm 3.22 docs (latest v3 on helm.sh; pinned 3.19).

using_helm: "An upgrade takes an existing release and upgrades it according to the information you provide." "Every time an install, upgrade, or rollback happens, the revision number is incremented by 1." "The first revision number is always 1." changes_since_helm2: Helm 3 lets the client "render the Charts client-side, and store a record of the installation in Kubernetes." Execution (outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/helm-release.txt): install REVISION: 1, upgrade REVISION: 2.

helm_history example table header: "REVISION    UPDATED    STATUS    CHART    APP VERSION    DESCRIPTION", rows 1-3 "superseded", row 4 "deployed". Captured run at stage-3: after upgrade, 1 superseded / 2 deployed.

Round 2: lesson §4, §6 and summary line 3 now say "By default" and "chart and values". advanced/Storage backends: "Helm 3 changed the default release information storage to Secrets in the namespace of the release." "The release information includes the contents of charts and values files". A Secret is an API object, so writing/reading it goes through the API server.

Execution, captured run at stage-3: "sh.helm.release.v1.web.v1   helm.sh/release.v1" and "sh.helm.release.v1.web.v2   helm.sh/release.v1". Helm docs pages opened (changes_since_helm2, advanced) do not state the naming; verdict rests on the run output only.

changes_since_helm2: "In Helm 3, information about a particular release is now stored in the same namespace as the release itself." Tiller removed; the client stores "a record of the installation in Kubernetes." No local release store is documented; any client with access to those Secrets reads the same record.

helm_rollback: "This command rolls back a release to a previous revision." using_helm: "Every time an install, upgrade, or rollback happens, the revision number is incremented by 1." Captured run: "3   deployed   web-0.1.0   Rollback to 1", revision 2 "superseded". Caveat: helm_rollback/helm_upgrade --history-max "limit the maximum number of revisions saved per release ... (default 10)" (see minor issue on §6).

helm_rollback synopsis: "The first argument of the rollback command is the name of a release, and the second is a revision (version) number." The command takes no chart path, so it has nothing local to write; it acts on the stored release. The script comment (lines 41-44) states the same.

helm_uninstall: "It removes all of the resources associated with the last release of the chart as well as the release history"; --keep-history: "remove all associated resources and mark the release as deleted, but retain the release history". using_helm: "In Helm 3, deletion removes the release record as well."

Captured run at stage-3 matches: REVISION 1 / replicas: 1; REVISION 2 / replicas: 2; after rollback replicas: 1; after uninstall "No resources found in helm-lessons namespace." deploy/helm/lessons/web/values.yaml@stage-3: "replicas: 1".

Round 2: lesson §5 now matches. helm_install/helm_rollback --wait: "will wait until all Pods, PVCs, Services, and minimum number of Pods of a Deployment, StatefulSet, or ReplicaSet are in a ready state before marking the release as successful. It will wait for as long as --timeout". helm_uninstall --wait: "will wait until all the resources are deleted before returning".

helm-release.sh lines 8-9: helm() adds "--kube-context kind-donhang-staging", kubectl() adds "--context kind-donhang-staging"; line 11 replicas reads '{.spec.replicas}'; line 15 awk prints $1 $3 $4 $6 (drops UPDATED and APP VERSION); lines 26/29 grep '^NAME' '^REVISION' '^STATUS'. Captured header: "REVISION   STATUS   CHART   DESCRIPTION". Prose wording on how the context is chosen: see minor issue on §5.
helm_history example rows show CHART as "alpine-0.1.0" (name-version). Chart.yaml@stage-3: "name: web", "version: 0.1.0". Captured run: CHART "web-0.1.0" in all three rows.

Round 2: §7 no longer quotes an error message. Supported: helm_uninstall removes "the release history"; using_helm "deletion removes the release record as well"; helm_history inherited flag "--kube-context string   name of the kubeconfig context to use". Not documented: that helm history exits with an error for a missing release. Could not run helm in this session (shell commands not permitted); captured output stops before Try it step 2. Kind behavior, not blocking.

refs/kubernetes-website deployment.md: "Now you've decided to undo the current rollout and rollback to the previous revision:" followed by "kubectl rollout undo deployment/nginx-deployment". The command targets one Deployment object and operates on the cluster, not on files.

issues.text: New in round 2 (changed text; the wording came from the round-1 fix). "it removes none" is too absolute: helm_rollback documents --history-max "limit the maximum number of revisions saved per release ... (default 10)", so a rollback that creates revision 11 prunes the oldest. The bad revision (the one just replaced) does stay, so the bullet's point holds.
issues.quote: because a rollback only adds a revision; it removes none.
issues.fix: Replace with "because a rollback adds a new revision instead of deleting the one it replaces." Do not introduce --history-max (outside depth_notes).

issues.text: New in round 2 (changed text). The script does not select (switch) the kubeconfig context: lines 7-9 wrap helm and kubectl to pass --kube-context / --context kind-donhang-staging on every call, "whatever context is current". "by selecting the kubeconfig context" can be read as `kubectl config use-context`.
issues.fix: Replace with "by passing the kubeconfig context `kind-donhang-staging` to every `helm` (`--kube-context`) and `kubectl` (`--context`) call, without changing your current context".
